question: If a firm keeps records of its outsourcing arrangements and can share outsourcing and third party information the PRA would reasonably expect, when can the PRA still require specific outsourcing information or documents, and what test does the PRA use to decide it can ask?
expected_answer: A firm is expected to keep appropriate records of its outsourcing arrangements and to make available to the PRA information on its outsourcing and third party arrangements that the PRA would reasonably expect notice of, so the firm should be prepared to provide records and related information about those arrangements when needed [#SRC:ff27a2b6ca15a12d]. Separately, the PRA is permitted to require certain persons to provide specified information (or information of a specified description) and specified documents (or documents of a specified description) where the PRA considers that what it is asking for is, or might be, relevant to the stability of one or more aspects of the UK financial system [#TGT:b90d21dd49fd907e]. So, even if the firm already has outsourcing records and can share expected outsourcing/third-party information, the PRA can still make a more formal, specific request for particular information or documents about outsourcing arrangements. The deciding test is the PRA’s view that the requested material is, or might be, relevant to UK financial system stability, and the request can be tailored by naming the exact items or describing the type of information or documents required.
source_text: The PRA expects all firms to keep appropriate records of their outsourcing arrangements. The PRA considers that a firm, in complying with 2.3(1)(e) of the Notifications Part of the PRA Rulebook, would likely already have records of its material outsourcing arrangements for this purpose. The records should also be sufficient to enable the firm to fulfil the expectations concerning concentration risk set out in 5.24 . Firms should also make any information on their outsourcing and third party arrangements of which the PRA would reasonably expect notice available to it in accordance with Fundamental Rule 7 . The PRA may, if appropriate and justified, also request data on firms’ outsourcing arrangements under section 165 of FSMA. 34
target_text: 34. The PRA may exercise, under section 165A of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA), the power to require certain persons to provide (i) specified information or information of a specified description; or (ii) specified documents or documents of a specified description, that it considers are, or might be, relevant to the stability of one or more aspects of the UK financial system (the financial stability information power).

question: If a participating Solvency II undertaking sits under another Solvency II undertaking or an insurance holding company or mixed financial holding company with its head office in the UK or Gibraltar, at what level in the group must the firms make sure eligible own funds in the group always cover the group SCR?
expected_answer: When the participating Solvency II undertaking (or the insurance holding company or mixed financial holding company) is itself a subsidiary undertaking of another Solvency II undertaking or of another insurance holding company or mixed financial holding company that has its head office in the UK or Gibraltar, the relevant group requirements apply only at the level of the ultimate Solvency II undertaking, insurance holding company, or mixed financial holding company in the group that has its head office in the UK or Gibraltar [#SRC:5d7d86c6c088b08d]. Where the relevant condition applies, each participating Solvency II undertaking that is a firm in the group and each relevant insurance group undertaking must ensure that eligible own funds are available in the group and that those eligible own funds are always at least equal to the group SCR (with the group SCR calculated under the applicable group SCR calculation provisions) [#TGT:17dc5c7d4f47f6cd]. Putting these together, the “always cover the group SCR” requirement is treated as a group-level requirement that is applied at the ultimate UK or Gibraltar-headed level when the specified parent-subsidiary structure exists, rather than being applied separately at each lower subsidiary layer, while still requiring the identified firms and relevant insurance group undertakings to ensure the group maintains that coverage on an ongoing basis.
source_text: If the participating Solvency II undertaking or the insurance holding company or mixed financial holding company referred to in 2.1(1) or 2.1(2) is itself a subsidiary undertaking of another Solvency II undertaking or of another insurance holding company or mixed financial holding company which has its head office in the UK or Gibraltar, then 4 to 19 apply only at the level of the ultimate Solvency II undertaking , insurance holding company , or mixed financial holding company in the group which has its head office in the UK or Gibraltar.
target_text: Where 2.1(1) applies, each participating Solvency II undertaking that is a firm in the group and each relevant insurance group undertaking must ensure that eligible own funds are available in the group which are always at least equal to the group SCR as calculated in accordance with 7 to 12 .

question: When applying the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA)’s supervisory expectations on combined buffers, how should a firm determine what constitutes its combined buffer, including which component buffers are included and when any systemic risk element applies, and how do the PRA’s capital buffers rules address the framework for capital conservation measures if the firm does not meet that combined buffer?
expected_answer: A firm should treat the PRA’s supervisory statement as setting supervisory expectations and providing clarifications on how the combined buffers regime is to be understood and applied in practice, alongside the underlying requirements it complements [#SRC:0b1108eeae5c69a4]. In determining what constitutes the firm’s combined buffer, the firm should identify the component buffers that make up the combined buffer: the capital conservation buffer (CCoB), the countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB), the buffer for Global Systemically Important Institutions (G-SII buffer), the buffer for other systemically important institutions (O-SII buffer), and the systemic risk buffer where it is applicable to the firm [#TGT:3c017bee1329df66]. The systemic risk buffer is included only on the condition that it applies to the firm, so the firm’s combined buffer composition depends on whether that applicability condition is met [#TGT:3c017bee1329df66]. Where a firm does not meet its combined buffer, the relevant frameworks for the CCoB, the CCyB, and the associated capital conservation measures are set out in the PRA’s capital buffers rules, which the supervisory statement indicates it complements and clarifies [#SRC:0b1108eeae5c69a4] [#TGT:3c017bee1329df66].
source_text: The purpose of this supervisory statement is to set out the expectations of the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) on the combined buffers and provide some clarifications of the PRA rules. 1 This statement complements the requirements set out in Title VII Chapter 4 of the CRD and the Capital Buffers Part of the PRA Rulebook and the high-level expectations on capital outlined in The PRA’s approach to banking supervision. 2
target_text: The combined buffer will include the capital conservation buffer (CCoB), the countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB), the buffer for Global Systemically Important Institutions (G-SII buffer) , the buffer for other systemically important institutions (O-SII buffer) and the systemic risk buffer — if applicable to a firm, as required by CRD. The frameworks for the CCoB, the CCyB and capital conservation measures when a firm does not meet its combined buffer are set out in the PRA’s capital buffers rules.

question: When Solvency II undertakings in a group are subsidiary undertakings of an insurance holding company or a mixed financial holding company, what must each relevant insurance group undertaking do to ensure that eligible own funds are available at the level where group solvency is calculated, and what minimum relationship must those own funds have to the group SCR?
expected_answer: Where Solvency II undertakings in a group are subsidiary undertakings of an insurance holding company or a mixed financial holding company, the group’s solvency calculation must be performed at the level of that insurance holding company or mixed financial holding company, using the specified approach for calculating group solvency [#TGT:bfadda41c802247a]. In that context, each relevant insurance group undertaking has an ongoing obligation to ensure that eligible own funds are available within the group and that those eligible own funds are not merely sufficient at a point in time but remain at least equal to the group SCR as calculated under the applicable group SCR methodology [#SRC:0242fd8e190ad528]. Read together, this means the solvency calculation performed at the holding company level must be supported by the group’s continuous maintenance of eligible own funds at or above the calculated group SCR, with responsibility placed on each relevant insurance group undertaking to ensure availability of those funds across the group [#TGT:bfadda41c802247a] [#SRC:0242fd8e190ad528].
source_text: Where 2.1(2) applies, each relevant insurance group undertaking must ensure that eligible own funds are available in the group which are always at least equal to the group SCR as calculated in accordance with 14 .
target_text: (1) Where Solvency II undertakings in a group are subsidiary undertakings of an insurance holding company or a mixed financial holding company , the calculation of the solvency of the group must be carried out at the level of the insurance holding company or mixed financial holding company applying 7.1(2) to 12 .

question: If a ring-fenced body regularly gets services or facilities from an entity in its group, how can the firm use its existing intragroup outsourcing compliance and OCIR record-keeping to help show it can only use that group entity when it is allowed to supply those services?
expected_answer: A firm can use work it has already done for intragroup outsourcing arrangements to help meet related obligations and expectations, instead of treating the intragroup setup as entirely new compliance. The source explains that, where relevant, firms may be able to leverage compliance with existing requirements in other regulatory areas for intragroup outsourcing arrangements, and that meeting those requirements may also help meet expectations around matters such as business continuity and exit plans [#SRC:085af7075bdc3067]. Separately, the target sets a specific permission with a condition: when a ring-fenced body receives services and accesses facilities it needs on a regular basis from an entity in its group, it may do so (directly or indirectly) only if that entity is a permitted supplier [#TGT:3bda544205c32b66]. To connect these, the firm should use elements of its operational continuity in resolution record-keeping to identify and document intragroup dependencies and keep the relevant information clear and readily available to the PRA upon request [#SRC:085af7075bdc3067]. That documentation can then support demonstrating that the regular group provider is treated consistently with the permitted-supplier condition for the ring-fenced body’s arrangements [#TGT:3bda544205c32b66].
source_text: Where relevant, firms may be able to leverage compliance with existing requirements in other areas of regulation to help meet their regulatory obligations in respect of their intragroup outsourcing arrangements. For instance, for some banks, intragroup outsourcing arrangements may be subject to the requirements in Operational Continuity Chapter 4 and Chapters 9 and 12 in the Ring-Fenced Bodies Part of the PRA Rulebook. Compliance with these requirements may also mean those banks meet certain expectations in this SS in respect of intragroup outsourcing arrangements (for instance, in respect of business continuity and exit plans (see Chapter 10 )). The PRA also expects firms to consider whether they can leverage elements of their operational continuity in resolution (OCIR) record-keeping to identify and document their intragroup dependencies, as long as relevant information is clear and readily available to the PRA upon request. 23
target_text: (1) Where a ring-fenced body receives services and accesses facilities that it requires on a regular basis from an entity in its group , it may do so, whether directly or indirectly, only where that entity is a permitted supplier .

question: For firms in scope of Solvency II (including the Society of Lloyd's) and the auditors of those firms, how should references to EU or EU-derived legislation be interpreted when applying the expectations on external audit assurance over the Solvency and Financial Condition Report and the governing body’s approval responsibilities, and what scope limitation applies for certain small insurers or small groups?
expected_answer: When applying this supervisory statement to firms in scope of Solvency II (including the Society of Lloyd’s) and to the auditors of those firms, EU or EU‑derived legislative references should be read as referring to the version of that legislation that was retained in the UK, unless the supervisory statement explicitly states otherwise [#TGT:b7e22a03a0d31c77]. This interpretive point frames how firms and auditors should understand any EU‑based terminology or requirements that appear in the supervisory statement’s expectations. Within that scope, the supervisory statement reminds the governing body that it is responsible for ensuring the ongoing appropriateness of information disclosed and that it must approve the Solvency and Financial Condition Report (SFCR), and it sets out the level of assurance expected for the external audit requirement on the SFCR as well as the audit guidance the PRA expects auditors to follow when auditing a firm’s SFCR [#SRC:f6eda4656f8eb76e]. However, the parts of the supervisory statement that relate to the external audit of the SFCR do not apply to ‘small insurers for external audit purposes’ and ‘small groups for external audit purposes’, so those entities are outside the applicability boundary for the external-audit-specific expectations even though the broader interpretive approach to EU references still governs how the supervisory statement is read [#SRC:f6eda4656f8eb76e] [#TGT:b7e22a03a0d31c77].
source_text: This Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) supervisory statement is relevant to firms in scope of Solvency II, including the Society of Lloyd's (collectively 'insurers' or ‘firms’ throughout the SS), and the auditors of those firms. 1 It reminds the governing body of its responsibilities in respect of the ongoing appropriateness of the information disclosed, and that it must approve the Solvency and Financial Condition Report (SFCR). It also sets out the level of assurance expected with respect to the external audit requirement on the SFCR and the audit guidance that the PRA expects auditors to follow in auditing a firm’s SFCR. It should be read alongside the External Auditors Part of the PRA Rulebook. The parts of this supervisory statement that relate to the external audit of the SFCR are not applicable to 'small insurers for external audit purposes' and 'small groups for external audit purposes', as set out in External Audit 1.1 .
target_text: 1. Unless otherwise stated, any references to EU or EU derived legislation in this SS refer to the version of that legislation which forms part of the body of law that was retained in the UK.

question: When a firm is considering whether it must not submit a PRA senior management approval application for a person unless it is satisfied the person is fit and proper for the relevant PRA senior management function, how should the matters referred to be treated in relation to the PRA’s determination of that person’s fitness and propriety?
expected_answer: A firm is prohibited from making a PRA senior management approval application for a person unless the firm is satisfied that the person is fit and proper to perform the PRA senior management function covered by the application [#TGT:27965488ad9f0cda]. In reaching and evidencing that satisfaction, the firm should recognise that the matters referred to are relevant to the PRA’s own determination of whether the person to whom the application relates is fit and proper [#SRC:268a1073ad54dc5e]. Read together, this means the firm’s pre-submission assessment should be aligned to the factors the PRA will consider when it determines fitness and propriety for the same individual and application context. Practically, the firm should ensure its internal evaluation addresses those relevant matters so that its “satisfied” conclusion is supportable in light of the PRA’s determination process, and it should avoid submitting the application where those matters would prevent it from being satisfied as to the person’s fitness and propriety for the specific function [#TGT:27965488ad9f0cda] while acknowledging their relevance to the PRA’s assessment [#SRC:268a1073ad54dc5e].
source_text: The matters referred to in 2 are relevant to the PRA’s determination of whether a person to whom a PRA senior management approval application relates is fit and proper.
target_text: A firm must not make a PRA senior management approval application in relation to a person unless it is satisfied that person is fit and proper to perform the PRA senior management function to which the application relates.

question: If a firm is making its first MA application to the PRA, what does it need to include to show it meets the MA eligibility conditions, and what extra information should it add if it thinks the PRA will need it to make a decision—especially if the firm wants to include guaranteed elements of with-profits annuities in its MA portfolio(s)?
expected_answer: For an initial MA application, the firm needs to provide the PRA with what it needs to be satisfied that the firm meets the MA eligibility conditions. This includes written confirmation that the firm complies with those eligibility conditions and, for conditions where it is expected, documentary evidence to support that written confirmation [#TGT:706be7f8963a27d5]. Alongside these eligibility confirmations and supporting documents, the firm should also make sure the application includes any other information not otherwise listed that the firm considers necessary for the PRA’s assessment and decision [#SRC:ec76fc94f0d3a021]. This means the firm should not limit itself only to the specified confirmations and evidence if there are additional facts, explanations, or materials that it believes the PRA will need to assess the application properly [#SRC:ec76fc94f0d3a021]. If the firm is seeking to include any guaranteed elements of with-profits annuities in its MA portfolio(s), the PRA would expect the application to include confirmation that the firm has considered the implications for its with-profits business (including fairness, investment strategy, and wider management) and, where necessary, has discussed those implications with the FCA [#SRC:ec76fc94f0d3a021] [#TGT:706be7f8963a27d5].
source_text: In addition to the above, a firm should ensure (in line with paragraph 2.6 above) that the application includes any other information (not explicitly mentioned in paragraphs 2.7 to 2.9 above) that it considers necessary for the assessment and decision by the PRA. Where a firm is seeking to include any guaranteed elements of with-profits annuities in its MA portfolio(s), the PRA would expect the application to include confirmation that the firm has satisfied itself that any implications for its with-profits business (including points around fairness, investment strategy and wider management) have been considered and, if necessary, discussed with the FCA.

question: If the PRA publishes a statement to explain its general approach more clearly, how should it use feedback from a public consultation, and what should it avoid changing when it accepts suggested wording changes?
expected_answer: When the PRA publishes a statement to expand on its general approach, it is doing so to clearly and consistently explain its views in order to advance its objectives for the firms it regulates and to support protection for policyholders [#TGT:6513a735d431f5ba]. If that statement has been subject to public consultation and reflects feedback received by the PRA, the PRA can take account of comments by accepting suggested changes to the wording where those changes improve clarity [#SRC:f7de2cea26e343cf]. However, the PRA should treat these accepted edits as clarifications only and avoid changing the underlying policy as a result of the consultation feedback [#SRC:f7de2cea26e343cf]. In other words, consultation feedback can be used to make the statement easier to understand and more precise, but it should not be used to introduce a policy change. This keeps the statement aligned with its purpose of explaining the PRA’s views clearly and consistently to support its objectives [#TGT:6513a735d431f5ba], while ensuring that any updates prompted by consultation remain limited to wording improvements rather than substantive policy revisions [#SRC:f7de2cea26e343cf].
source_text: The statement was subject to public consultation, 1 and reflects feedback received by the PRA. Some comments suggested altering wording and these suggestions have been accepted where clarity would be improved. There is no change in policy.
target_text: The PRA is publishing this statement to expand on its general approach as set out in its Insurance Approach document. 2 By clearly and consistently explaining its views in this area, the PRA seeks to advance its statutory objectives of ensuring the safety and soundness of the firms it regulates, and contributing to securing an appropriate degree of protection for policyholders.

question: If a firm is doing benchmarking activities and the relevant provisions generally do not apply to it for those activities (unless they were made before IP completion day to transpose an EU instrument), what compliance and financial-crime policies and procedures must the firm keep in place for its managers, employees and appointed representatives (or tied agents where applicable)?
expected_answer: For a firm carrying on benchmarking activities, the key scope point is that the relevant provisions do not apply to the firm in respect of those activities, except to the extent that, before IP completion day, they were made for the purpose of transposing an EU instrument [#SRC:5ccfd157f8a1ab18]. Even with that limitation, the firm must establish, implement and maintain adequate policies and procedures that are sufficient to ensure the firm’s compliance with its obligations under the regulatory system [#TGT:5ca4886f7aeb4304]. Those policies and procedures must cover not only the firm itself but also its managers, employees and appointed representatives, and where applicable, tied agents [#TGT:5ca4886f7aeb4304]. In addition, the firm’s policies and procedures must be aimed at countering the risk that the firm might be used to further financial crime [#TGT:5ca4886f7aeb4304]. In practice, the firm should align its compliance controls to whatever obligations remain applicable given the benchmarking-activity carve-out and the pre-IP completion day EU-transposition exception, while ensuring the covered people and representatives follow the firm’s compliance and financial-crime risk controls [#SRC:5ccfd157f8a1ab18] [#TGT:5ca4886f7aeb4304].
source_text: 2.1 to 2.2B do not apply to a firm with respect to the carrying on of benchmarking activities except to the extent that before IP completion day , they were made for the purpose of transposing an EU instrument.
target_text: A firm must establish, implement and maintain adequate policies and procedures sufficient to ensure compliance of the firm including its managers, employees and appointed representatives (or where applicable, tied agents ) with its obligations under the regulatory system and for countering the risk that the firm might be used to further financial crime .

question: If Institutions have to publish information about their remuneration policy and practices for staff who can materially affect the Institutions’ risk profile, what template and instructions do they need to use for the disclosures linked to points (h)(i) and (h)(ii)?
expected_answer: Institutions are required to disclose information about their remuneration policy and practices for those categories of staff whose professional activities have a material impact on the Institutions’ risk profile [#TGT:d3efeb25748ccfe0]. Where the required remuneration disclosures include the items identified as points (h)(i) and (h)(ii), Institutions must not choose an arbitrary format; they must complete those disclosures using Template UK REM1 and follow the relevant instructions set out in the specified annex of instructions [#SRC:f75c4876ca123e11]. This links the general disclosure duty on remuneration policy and practices (focused on staff with a material impact on risk profile) with a concrete procedural requirement on how certain parts of that disclosure must be presented and completed. So, to comply, Institutions should (1) identify the relevant categories of staff covered by the disclosure obligation, and (2) for the specified disclosure points, populate Template UK REM1 in line with the accompanying instructions, ensuring the disclosed information is provided in the required structured way [#TGT:d3efeb25748ccfe0] [#SRC:f75c4876ca123e11].
source_text: (b) For the disclosures required in points (h)(i) and (h)(ii) of Article 450(1) of the CRR , in accordance with the Template UK REM1 of Annex XXXIII and the relevant instructions set out in Annex XXXIV .

question: If a firm has a matching adjustment permission and more than one SMF holds PR Q, who needs to sign the attestation sent to the PRA, and does it need to cover each relevant portfolio of assets the firm holds?
expected_answer: If the firm has a matching adjustment permission, it must send the required attestation to the PRA, and that attestation must be provided in respect of each relevant portfolio of assets as a whole held by the firm, following the required timing, person, and form requirements [#TGT:e4cd8736edad498d]. The person responsible for the attestation is the senior manager with the prescribed responsibility for the production and integrity of the firm’s financial information and its regulatory reporting (PR Q) [#SRC:60350a1cc8a674eb]. When more than one SMF holds PR Q, the PRA would expect all of those SMFs to attest, not just one of them, because each holder of PR Q is treated as having that prescribed responsibility [#SRC:60350a1cc8a674eb]. This expectation reflects that the relevant SMF(s) should have ultimate governance responsibility for the calculation underpinning the firm’s position, regardless of any delegation, and be able to implement an increase if required [#SRC:60350a1cc8a674eb]. So, the firm should arrange for all SMFs holding PR Q to provide the attestation that is submitted to the PRA and ensure it addresses each relevant portfolio as required [#TGT:e4cd8736edad498d].
source_text: Matching Adjustment 9.1(3) requires that the senior manager with the prescribed responsibility for the production and integrity of the firm’s financial information and its regulatory reporting (PR Q), as provided for in Rule 3.1(4) of the Insurance – Allocation of Responsibilities Part of the PRA Rulebook, will be responsible for the attestation. This is because the SMF should have ultimate governance responsibility for the calculation of the FS and MA (regardless of delegations of any of their responsibilities), and can therefore implement an increase to the FS if required. In many cases, this will be SMF 2, the Chief Financial Officer, but this could be another SMF depending on how responsibility is allocated within the firm. A firm should approach its usual supervisory contact, in the first instance, should its governance arrangements mean that an alternative SMF would be more appropriate to undertake the attestation. Where more than one SMF holds PR Q, the PRA would expect all of those SMFs to attest. The PRA considers that the supervisory guidance contained in SS35/15 – Strengthening individual accountability in insurance 25 on sharing prescribed responsibilities (in particular paragraph 2.19A of that SS) would also apply.
target_text: A firm with a matching adjustment permission must provide to the PRA the attestation set out at (1) at the time set out in (2) by a person in (3) in the form set out in 12.1 in respect of each relevant portfolio of assets as a whole held by the firm .

question: If a UK ISPV uses a special purpose vehicle in Gibraltar or a third country, what does that vehicle need to have in place with a supervisory authority and equivalent requirements, and what kind of governance system must the UK ISPV have for its own management and risks?
expected_answer: When a UK ISPV uses a special purpose vehicle in Gibraltar or a third country, the special purpose vehicle must be regulated by a supervisory authority in Gibraltar or in the relevant third country, and it must comply with requirements that are equivalent to the specified set of requirements referenced for these vehicles [#SRC:012c29b081ac0f05]. Separately, the UK ISPV must have an effective system of governance that supports the sound and prudent management of the UK ISPV, and that system must be appropriate to the nature, scale, and complexity of the risks the UK ISPV assumes and to the regulated activity for which it is authorised [#TGT:d90fd8705cd51108]. In practice, compliance requires both elements at the same time: confirming the external vehicle’s supervision and equivalence, and ensuring the UK ISPV’s own governance is robust enough to manage the risks and authorised activity associated with that arrangement [#SRC:012c29b081ac0f05] [#TGT:d90fd8705cd51108].
source_text: (2) in the case of a special purpose vehicle in Gibraltar or a third country , it is regulated by a supervisory authority in Gibraltar or a third country , and complies with requirements equivalent to those set out in Insurance Special Purpose Vehicles 2 , 2A to 2D , and 5A.1 to 5A.4 .
target_text: A UK ISPV must have an effective system of governance which provides for the sound and prudent management of the UK ISPV and which is appropriate to the nature, scale and complexity of the risks it assumes and the regulated activity for which it is authorised.

question: If you are one of the people that these provisions apply to, what do you have to do when you delegate your responsibilities to someone else?
expected_answer: This delegation requirement applies only to a person who is within the specific group that the provisions say they apply to; if you are not in that group, the requirement described here does not apply to you under those provisions [#SRC:e5d9bc4b52307125]. If you are in scope, you must take reasonable steps when you delegate any of your responsibilities. Those steps must ensure (1) you delegate to an appropriate person, and (2) you oversee how that delegated responsibility is carried out effectively [#TGT:003c4c76cc9a33c5]. So, you cannot simply hand off a task and assume it will be handled correctly; you need to make a reasonable judgment that the person you choose is appropriate for what you are delegating, and you must keep effective oversight of how they discharge that responsibility after it has been delegated. The obligation is expressed as taking reasonable steps, which means your actions should be sufficient to show you actively ensured appropriateness at the time of delegation and maintained effective oversight of the delegated work, but only where the provisions apply to you in the first place [#SRC:e5d9bc4b52307125] and as required for delegation and oversight [#TGT:003c4c76cc9a33c5].
source_text: (3) 3.1 to 3.3 only apply to a person in (2)(a), (b), or (f).
target_text: Senior Manager Conduct Rule 3 : You must take reasonable steps to ensure that any delegation of your responsibilities is to an appropriate person and that you oversee the discharge of the delegated responsibility effectively.

question: If the PRA is comparing a firm’s SA risk weights to an IRB benchmark to help set the firm’s Pillar 2A credit risk capital, what does the benchmark “range” mean, and what is different for CRE?
expected_answer: The PRA’s approach to informing the setting of firms’ Pillar 2A capital requirement for credit risk is to compare firms’ SA risk weights at a portfolio level against an IRB risk-weight benchmark, using benchmarks the PRA has calculated for portfolios such as mortgages (split into LTV bands), credit cards, corporates, sovereigns and institutions [#SRC:0289bd156b15ee1d]. In that context, the “range” around the benchmark is defined as a plus/minus 15% band, and it should not be treated as simply the spread you would get by looking at IRB firms’ average risk weights [#TGT:27afc0da558bb3b9]. There is one stated exception: for CRE, the possible range is the full range of risk weights outlined for CRE, rather than the plus/minus 15% concept [#TGT:27afc0da558bb3b9]. Separately, the PRA also distinguishes between two benchmark sets—one based on both unexpected and expected losses and another based on unexpected losses only, with the unexpected-loss-only set applying to firms using International Financial Reporting Standards where 12 months’ expected credit losses may already be covered by the SA Pillar 1 capital charge [#SRC:0289bd156b15ee1d].
source_text: The methodology used to inform the setting of firms’ Pillar 2A capital requirement for credit risk is based on a comparison of firms’ SA risk weights at a portfolio level to an IRB risk-weight benchmark. The PRA has created two sets of benchmarks. One is calculated based on both unexpected and expected losses (see Table A1 ). The other is based on unexpected losses only (see Table A2 ). The latter applies to firms using International Financial Reporting Standards and for which 12 months’ expected credit losses may already be covered by the SA Pillar 1 capital charge. Benchmarks have been calculated for mortgages (distinguished by loan to value (LTV) bands into fourteen categories), credit cards (both domestic and international), corporates, sovereigns and institutions (the latter two mapped to credit quality steps).
target_text: 6. The range stated is /- 15% and is not the simple range of IRB firms’ average risk weights, with the exception of the possible range for CRE which is the full range of risk weights outlined by CRR Articles 153(5) and 158(6).

question: Where the PRA would treat a communication as “advertising materials” because it contains an invitation to make a deposit or information intended (or reasonably presumed intended) to lead directly or indirectly to making a deposit, what must a firm not include in that communication regarding the deposit guarantee scheme, and what limited references are permitted?
expected_answer: If a communication falls within what the PRA considers “advertising materials”—because it contains an invitation to make a deposit, or includes information intended (or that might reasonably be presumed intended) to lead directly or indirectly to the making of a deposit, including any means of bringing such an invitation or information to the notice of the persons addressed [#SRC:be6058c4cbea740a]—a firm must not provide any further information about the deposit guarantee scheme within that advertising material beyond tightly limited statements [#TGT:965fc1eca462336c]. Specifically, the firm must not go beyond referring to the fact that the product advertised is or is not covered by the deposit guarantee scheme, except that it may also include any further factual information required by law (including by the applicable requirements referenced in the prohibition) [#TGT:965fc1eca462336c]. In practice, once the content or delivery method is captured by the PRA’s broad definition of advertising materials, the firm’s deposit guarantee scheme messaging must be confined to coverage status and legally required factual disclosures, and it must not add explanatory, promotional, comparative, or other additional scheme-related information in the same advertising materials [#SRC:be6058c4cbea740a] [#TGT:965fc1eca462336c].
source_text: In Depositor Protection 18.1 , the PRA considers ‘advertising materials’ to include any materials containing an invitation to make a deposit, or information that is intended or might reasonably be presumed to be intended to lead directly or indirectly to the making of a deposit; and includes any means of bringing such an invitation or such information to the notice of the person or persons to whom it is addressed.
target_text: A firm must not, in advertising materials, provide any further information about the deposit guarantee scheme beyond referring to the fact that the product advertised is or is not covered by the deposit guarantee scheme , and to any further factual information required by law including by this Part.

question: When a firm has more material exposure and is therefore expected to use greater skills and expertise among the persons involved in valuing assets, what must the firm have in place to ensure its valuation estimates of assets and liabilities remain reliable and appropriate for compliance purposes, and how will the PRA take the firm’s internal control of asset valuation into account when assessing valuation uncertainty risk management?
expected_answer: Where a firm’s exposure is more material, the PRA expects the persons involved in valuing the firm’s assets to have correspondingly greater skills and expertise, reflecting the increased demands of managing valuation uncertainty risk [#SRC:4937d12fd4d0c0ae]. In parallel, the firm must maintain effective systems and controls so that its valuation estimates for both assets and liabilities are reliable and appropriate for compliance with the applicable valuation requirements [#TGT:847d4c0d71170a5f]. In assessing the firm’s management of valuation uncertainty risk for compliance purposes, the PRA will consider the extent to which the firm meets the requirements relating to internal control over the valuation of assets, so the firm should be able to demonstrate that its governance and control environment supports robust valuation outcomes [#SRC:4937d12fd4d0c0ae]. Taken together, this means the firm should align the competence of the individuals performing or overseeing valuations with the materiality of its exposure, and ensure those individuals operate within a control framework that produces valuation estimates that are dependable and suitable for compliance [#TGT:847d4c0d71170a5f].
source_text: When assessing a firm’s management of valuation uncertainty risk for the purposes of complying with the PPP, the PRA will also consider the extent to which the firm satisfies the requirements under Conditions Governing Business 11D relating to the internal control of valuation of assets. The PRA expects that the more material the firm’s exposure, the greater the skills and expertise that will be required of the persons involved in the valuation of these assets.

question: If Firms can pick any audit method for outsourcing, what do they still need to make sure the method achieves, and how should they scale their approach based on the firm’s size and the importance of the outsourced function?
expected_answer: Firms are permitted to choose any audit method that is appropriate, but only if it enables them to meet their legal, regulatory, operational resilience, and risk management obligations [#SRC:f2bff782c4f63cad]. Separately, Firms should meet the expectations in this SS in a way that fits their size and internal organisation, the nature, scope, and complexity of their activities, and the criticality or importance of the outsourced function, following the principle of proportionality [#TGT:4a6318294bc51b91]. Put together, this means Firms should not treat “any audit method” as a free choice without constraints: the method must be capable of supporting the firm’s obligations, and the depth of assurance should be scaled to what is being outsourced and how important it is. As the arrangement becomes more material or the outsourced function more critical or important, Firms should increase the level of assurance they seek from the audit method so that it remains appropriate to the risks and to the SS expectations [#SRC:f2bff782c4f63cad] [#TGT:4a6318294bc51b91].
source_text: Firms can choose any appropriate audit method as long as it enables them to meet their legal, regulatory, operational resilience, and risk management obligations. The level of assurance expected will, however, become more onerous depending on proportionality (ie whether the firm is significant (see Chapter 3 )) and the materiality of the arrangement (see Chapter 5 ). For instance, a significant firm that outsources an important business service for which it has set a low impact tolerance should demand a higher level of assurance.
target_text: Firms should meet the expectations in this SS in a manner appropriate to: their size and internal organisation; the nature, scope, and complexity of their activities; and the criticality or importance of the outsourced function, in line with the principle of proportionality.

question: If a firm reports TMTP to the PRA only in certain reporting periods (and waivers may change that), what does it have to do about recalculating W r on the day it updates M in the TMTP method, including after a transfer event, and how does that fit with doing TMTP calculations more often for internal management?
expected_answer: The firm should first identify the “reporting period” as the reporting periods in which it is required to report TMTP to the PRA under the relevant reporting requirements, as adjusted by any waivers that apply to the firm’s reporting duties [#SRC:5324f23bfbfa472e]. Even though reporting happens in those defined periods, the firm also has a separate, specific timing requirement for W r: whenever it updates the value of M used in the TMTP method, it must, on that same day, calculate a new value of W r, and it must also do so following any transfer event [#TGT:abeb9eaab95b7d3d]. This means the W r recalculation is triggered by the update of M and by transfer events, not only by the calendar of reporting periods [#TGT:abeb9eaab95b7d3d]. The firm may still calculate TMTP more frequently for internal management if it wants to, but that is optional and does not change what counts as a reporting period for PRA reporting or the requirement to recalculate W r on the day M is updated and after transfer events [#SRC:5324f23bfbfa472e] [#TGT:abeb9eaab95b7d3d].

question: When using this SoP alongside the IRPR regulations and the relevant parts of the PRA Rulebook and related supervisory statements, where should an Applicant look for procedural guidance on how to make an application, and how does that relate to accessing the Prudential Person Principle supervisory statement referenced by the PRA?
expected_answer: Where an Applicant is relying on this SoP in conjunction with the IRPR regulations, the relevant parts of the PRA Rulebook, and the related supervisory statements it lists, the procedural direction for how to make an application is to use the Authorisations page on the PRA’s website as the place to find application-making information [#SRC:6f1cefbb88e9a396]. In parallel, when the Applicant needs to consult the supervisory statement on the Prudential Person Principle that is referenced among those related materials, it should access that supervisory statement via the Bank of England’s prudential regulation publication page provided for ‘Solvency II: Prudent Person Principle’ (June 2024) [#TGT:235eb5a2349a381c]. Taken together, the SoP indicates that application process guidance is obtained through the PRA’s Authorisations web content, while the substantive supervisory statement on the Prudential Person Principle is obtained through the linked publication page. This ensures the Applicant uses the correct PRA web route for application procedure and the correct Bank of England publication route for the referenced supervisory statement when assembling and supporting its application materials.
source_text: This SoP should be read in conjunction with the IRPR regulations, the Matching Adjustment Part of the PRA Rulebook, the Investments Part of the PRA Rulebook, the relevant rules in the rest of the Solvency II Sector of the PRA Rulebook, supervisory statement (SS) 7/18 – Solvency II: Matching adjustment 1 , SS1/20 – Solvency II: Prudent Person Principle 2 , SS8/18 – Solvency II: Internal models – modelling of the matching adjustment 3 , SS3/17 – Solvency II: Illiquid unrated assets 4 and the PRA’s insurance approach document. 5 For information about making an application, see the Authorisations page of the PRA’s website.
target_text: 2. ‘Solvency II: Prudent Person Principle’, June 2024: www.bankofengland.co.uk/prudential-regulation/publication/2020/solvency-ii-prudent-person-principle-ss .

question: If a firm’s MA portfolio includes less liquid or non-traded assets, can it still use the matching adjustment, and does it need to apply the PRA’s expectations beyond corporate bond assets?
expected_answer: A firm can use the matching adjustment only if it has an MA permission from the PRA; without that permission it cannot apply the MA. With the permission, the firm is permitted to apply the MA to adjust the relevant risk-free interest rate term structure when calculating the best estimate for MA-eligible insurance or reinsurance obligations, and it may also use the MA for determining both technical provisions and the SCR [#SRC:c11c8099a431b8c8]. Where the MA portfolio contains a wide range of assets, including assets that are less liquid, more complex, or not traded, the firm should treat the PRA’s expectations as broader than just corporate bond holdings. While the expectations are described as primarily applying to risks from corporate bond assets, the PRA indicates that many expectations apply regardless of the assets held and should therefore be considered more widely applicable unless the statement says otherwise [#TGT:938b2dd2653608ec]. The firm should also pay attention to places where the statement sets specific expectations for less liquid assets, and apply those where relevant to its own MA portfolio holdings, recognising that further bespoke expectations for other asset types may be issued in future [#TGT:938b2dd2653608ec].
source_text: The MA allows firms to adjust the relevant risk-free interest rate term structure for the purpose of calculating the best estimate of a portfolio of MA-eligible insurance or reinsurance obligations. To apply an MA, firms must have an MA permission from the PRA, as per Matching Adjustment 2.1 . Firms with an MA permission are permitted to apply an MA for the purposes of determining both TPs and the SCR. The PRA expects firms to have confidence that the level of MA benefit assumed in each of these calculations is fit for purpose. The PRA’s expectations relating to modelling of the MA within the SCR calculation are set out in SS8/18 . These expectations primarily apply to the risks arising in respect of corporate bond assets within firms’ MA portfolios. However, the PRA recognises that many of the expectations in SS8/18 would apply regardless of the assets held (see paragraph 1.8 of SS8/18 ).
target_text: The PRA recognises that many firms hold a relatively wide range of assets in their MA portfolios. These assets will differ in terms of liquidity and complexity; many of them may not be traded assets. The PRA’s expectations set out in this statement primarily apply to the risks arising in respect of corporate bond assets within firms’ MA portfolios. However, many of the expectations apply irrespective of the assets held and the PRA would therefore expect firms to consider the expectations set out in the SS to be more widely applicable unless specifically stated otherwise. In a number of places (eg paragraphs 4.10 , 4.15 , 4.20 , 4.22 , 5.17 and 5.18 ) the SS sets out specific expectations in relation to less liquid assets. In future, the PRA may issue further, more bespoke, expectations for the SCR treatment of other assets within an MA portfolio, such as illiquid assets.

question: For the Prudential Regulation Authority’s supervisory expectations that evolve as non-systemic UK-incorporated banks grow from authorisation to being regarded as fully established banks, which firms fall within the defined category of “new banks” based on mobilisation status, authorisation restrictions, and the 12‑month timing since authorisation?
expected_answer: The Prudential Regulation Authority’s supervisory expectations described here apply to ‘new and growing’ non-systemic UK-incorporated banks (collectively referred to as ‘banks’) and are framed as evolving as those banks grow from the point of authorisation to being regarded as fully established banks [#SRC:1dd002d682527b05]. Within that scope, “new banks” are specifically the firms that are either (i) in the mobilisation stage, meaning they have authorisation with restrictions, or (ii) have received authorisation without restrictions within the past 12 months, including firms that have exited mobilisation or were authorised without using the mobilisation period [#TGT:ac9d92c59779a4e0]. Read together, this means a non-systemic UK-incorporated bank is treated as “new” for purposes of these evolving supervisory expectations when it is still operating under restricted authorisation during mobilisation, or when it has only recently moved to (or started with) unrestricted authorisation and remains within the first 12 months of that status. This definition helps determine when the bank is at the earliest stage of the growth path covered by the supervisory expectations, before it is regarded as fully established.
source_text: This Supervisory Statement (SS) provides an overview of how the Prudential Regulation Authority’s (PRA)’s supervisory expectations of ‘new 1 and growing 2 ’non-systemic 3 UK-incorporated banks 4 , 5 (collectively referred to as ‘banks’), evolve as they grow from the point of authorisation to being regarded as fully established banks.
target_text: 1. New banks refers to firms that are in the ‘mobilisation stage’ (authorisation with restrictions) and those that have received authorisation without restrictions within the past 12 months (e.g. exited mobilisation or authorised without using the mobilisation period).

question: If you are working out what reporting and disclosure is expected under this supervisory statement, how should you read those expectations in light of the PRA’s approach to transitional relief, and where can you find the directions and guidance you need to check?
expected_answer: You should interpret the reporting and disclosure expectations that are within the scope of this supervisory statement by taking into account the PRA’s approach to transitional relief as it is set out in a direction and accompanying guidance [#SRC:cddb9c1a2aa676c5]. That means you should not rely only on the supervisory statement wording when deciding what to report or disclose; you should read it together with the direction and guidance that explain the PRA’s approach to transitional relief, and then apply the expectations in a way that is consistent with that approach. To make sure you are using the correct materials, you should obtain the directions and accompanying guidance from the place where they are made available online, which is the Bank of England webpage that provides access to the directions and accompanying guidance on transitioning to post-exit rules and standards [#TGT:d1107d21ebab9777]. Checking that source helps ensure your interpretation aligns with the same direction and guidance referenced by the PRA.
source_text: The PRA has set out in a direction and accompanying guidance 5 the approach it is taking to transitional relief. The reporting and disclosure expectations in scope of this supervisory statement should be interpreted in light of the direction and guidance.
target_text: 5. The directions and accompanying guidance are available at: https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/eu-withdrawal/transitioning-to-post-exit-rules-and-standards .

question: If a derogation only changes the earlier valuation provisions and does not change the later valuation provisions except where they point back to the earlier ones for recognition or valuation, what does a firm have to do to recognise assets and liabilities, and when can the derogation affect that?
expected_answer: A firm must recognise assets and liabilities in conformity with UK-adopted international accounting standards, and it should do so while respecting the limited scope of the derogation described in the valuation framework. The scope text explains that the derogation relates to the earlier valuation provisions and does not affect the application of the later valuation provisions, except to the extent those later provisions refer back to the earlier valuation provisions for recognition or valuation. So the firm should continue to apply the later valuation provisions as normal, and only allow the derogation to influence outcomes where a later provision explicitly depends on the earlier valuation provisions for recognition or valuation. This keeps the firm’s recognition approach anchored in the accounting standards requirement [#TGT:0179241db33533af] while ensuring the derogation is not applied more widely than intended, and is used only for the specific cross-referenced recognition or valuation elements described in the scope statement [#SRC:53d338d2a0530445].
source_text: The derogation relates to Valuation 5.1 and 5.2 , but does not affect the application of Valuation 6 to 12 except to the extent that these provisions refer back to Valuation 5 regarding recognition or valuation. Therefore in addition to Valuation 5 :
target_text: A firm must recognise assets and liabilities in conformity with UK-adopted international accounting standards .

question: If a firm must safeguard the independence of the risk function and oversee how it performs (including the performance of a person approved to perform the Chief Risk function), what does the firm have to do to make sure the head of the risk management function is independent and properly appointed, and when can another senior person do that job instead?
expected_answer: The firm must put in place responsibility for safeguarding the independence of the risk function and for overseeing how the risk function performs, including overseeing the performance of a person approved to perform the Chief Risk function on behalf of the firm [#SRC:8c09718d22d2ff24]. At the same time, the firm must ensure that the head of the risk management function is an independent senior manager who has distinct responsibility for the risk management function [#TGT:2ec6e3f7d857bd07]. If the firm’s activities are such that their nature, scale and complexity do not justify having a specially appointed person as head, the firm may allow another senior person within the firm to fulfil that head-of-function role, but only if there is no conflict of interest [#TGT:2ec6e3f7d857bd07]. The firm must also ensure that the head of the risk management function cannot be removed unless the management body gives prior approval, and that the head can access the management body directly where necessary [#TGT:2ec6e3f7d857bd07]. These points collectively support the required independence and effective oversight of the risk function and the approved Chief Risk function holder [#SRC:8c09718d22d2ff24].
source_text: (17) responsibility for safeguarding the independence of, and overseeing of the performance of, the risk function , including the performance of a person approved to perform the Chief Risk function on behalf of the firm , in accordance with Risk Control 3.4 and 3.5 (PR L) ;
target_text: A firm must ensure that the head of the risk management function is an independent senior manager with distinct responsibility for the risk management function. Where the nature, scale and complexity of the activities of the firm do not justify a specially appointed person , another senior person within the firm may fulfil that function, provided there is no conflict of interest. A firm must ensure that the head of the risk management function must not be removed without prior approval of the management body and is able to have direct access to the management body where necessary.

question: If a firm has to explain whether its systems for meeting the requirement to mark eligible deposits so they can be identified immediately have been checked by auditors, what exactly must it say, and what must it add if the auditors did review the systems?
expected_answer: The firm must provide a statement saying whether the firm’s systems used to comply with the requirement to mark eligible deposits so they can be immediately identified have been reviewed by internal or external auditors [#TGT:60b306349873ce31]. This is about the firm’s compliance systems that support the marking and immediate identification of eligible deposits, not just the day-to-day act of marking deposits. If the firm’s systems have been reviewed, the firm must also include a statement of the findings from that review, meaning it must summarize what the internal or external auditors found when they assessed those systems [#SRC:64bec8980f6b4a13]. So the statement must cover two things: (1) whether an internal or external audit review happened, and (2) if it did happen, what the review concluded. The firm should ensure the statement clearly links the review and any findings to the systems that enable it to meet the marking requirement for eligible deposits.
source_text: (3) a statement of whether the firm’s systems to comply with 11.1 and 11.2 have been reviewed by internal or external auditors, and, if so, a statement of the findings of that review; and
target_text: A firm must mark eligible deposits in a way that allows for the immediate identification of such deposits .

question: If a firm uses an outsourcer for some or all of its internal credit assessment work, what does the PRA expect the firm to do so the outsourced assessments meet the PRA’s expanded expectations for internal credit assessments?
expected_answer: If a firm outsources some or all of its internal credit assessment process, it needs to ensure the outsourced internal credit assessments for assets meet the PRA’s expanded expectations for internal credit assessments [#SRC:e46640365e209635]. The PRA expects the firm to demonstrate that the outsourcer’s systems and processes are effective, and this includes showing that validation is in place and works as intended [#TGT:abeb4286e603ff85]. The firm should also be able to provide evidence that it has appropriate oversight systems and processes, including governance, for the outsourced credit assessments, and that these oversight arrangements have been carried out effectively in practice [#TGT:abeb4286e603ff85]. In other words, the firm should not treat outsourcing as transferring responsibility: it must be able to show both that the outsourced assessments align with the PRA’s expanded expectations and that the outsourcer’s methods are controlled, validated, and overseen through effective firm-led governance and monitoring [#SRC:e46640365e209635] [#TGT:abeb4286e603ff85].
source_text: [First sentence moved to 2.4B ] The PRA’s expectations for internal credit assessments are expanded on in paragraphs 2.8A to 2.8N below.
target_text: Where some or all of the internal credit assessment process is outsourced, the PRA expects firms also to demonstrate the effectiveness of the systems and processes that the outsourcer has in place, including validation, in order to ensure that outsourced internal credit assessments for assets satisfy the expectations set out in paragraphs 2.8A to 2.8M above and that the requirements of Rules 7.1A , 7.2A and 7.5 to 7.8 in the Conditions Governing Business Part of the PRA Rulebook are also satisfied. Firms should provide evidence that appropriate oversight systems and processes including governance are in place and have been carried out effectively for outsourced credit assessments.

question: When designing its policy for managing positions and collateral across relevant entities, what must a firm set out about the factors that determine when positions are offset or closed and the expected timeline for doing so, and how must it ensure it can identify legal and operational features that affect collateral management, including transfers within the group and to third parties?
expected_answer: A firm should document, in its policy, the specific factors it will use to decide when a position should be offset or closed, and it should also specify the expected timeline for taking those actions, so that position management is governed by clear decision criteria and time expectations [#SRC:0fc504dca2fa1201]. This policy should sit within effective, consolidated risk management oversight across the relevant entities and be calibrated to a level commensurate with the structure of the relevant business division, so that the consolidation point matches how seniority and reporting lines are organised [#SRC:0fc504dca2fa1201]. In parallel, the firm should be able to identify legal and operational features that impact the management of collateral, including features affecting the transfer of collateral both within the group and to third parties, so that collateral movements and constraints are understood and can be managed in practice [#TGT:08d9645cfabc4417]. Taken together, the policy’s decision factors and timelines for offsetting/closing positions should be operationally workable in light of those identified legal and operational constraints on collateral transfers [#SRC:0fc504dca2fa1201] [#TGT:08d9645cfabc4417].
source_text: d) effective, consolidated risk management oversight is in place across the relevant entities. This consolidated risk management should be set at a level that is commensurate with the structure of the relevant business division. As an example, if there are two senior business heads and they both report directly to the global business head, that would be the appropriate level. But if they are two more junior business heads, the consolidation should occur at a lower level. In addition, firms should consider what they need to manage their risks holistically both in business-as-usual and in a crisis. It is generally considered good practice to have a free flow of collateral between desks, and this is particularly helpful in a crisis so banks may be able to avoid hedging with the market externally unnecessarily. Similarly, there may be advantages to having the ability to reduce offsetting inventory positions by way of periodic inter-affiliate transactions, and the ability to pool collateral between entities and branches for centralised financing and short-covering purposes. The firm’s policy should set out the factors determining when a position should be offset or closed and the expected timeline for taking such actions. This approach is consistent with the Bank of England’s expectations under the UK Resolution Assessment Framework. 39
target_text: 39. Firms should also be able to identify any legal and operational features that impact the management of collateral, including the transfer of collateral both within the group and to third parties”. See Resolvability Assessment of Major UK Banks 2024. https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/financial-stability/resolution/resolvability-assessment-framework/resovability-assessment-of-major-uk-banks-2024

question: If an outsourcing deal is material and the PRA expects the written contract to cover areas like data security, audit and access rights, sub-outsourcing, and business continuity and exit, what do banks and insurers have to do about putting the outsourcing arrangement in writing?
expected_answer: Banks and insurers have to make sure the outsourcing arrangement is set out in a written agreement, and for material outsourcing that written agreement should cover the minimum areas the PRA expects. In practice, this means the firm should not only have a signed written contract for the outsourcing arrangement, but also ensure the contract includes terms dealing with data security, access, audit and information rights, sub-outsourcing, and business continuity and exit strategies, because these are identified as the minimum areas the PRA expects written agreements relating to material outsourcing to address [#SRC:7ee6ded449cc3c29]. Separately, there is a baseline requirement that all outsourcing arrangements must be set out in a written agreement for banks and insurers [#TGT:9752e97c411082aa]. Read together, the firm should treat the written agreement as the main control document: it must exist for every outsourcing arrangement, and for material outsourcing it should be detailed enough to cover the specific minimum topics the PRA expects.
source_text: Chapter 6 lists the areas that the PRA expects written agreements relating to material outsourcing to address as a minimum. The following four areas are then examined in detail in Chapters 7–10: data security ( Chapter 7 ); access, audit, and information rights ( Chapter 8 ); sub-outsourcing ( Chapter 9 ); and business continuity and exit strategies ( Chapter 10 ).
target_text: In line with Article 31(3) of MODR (banks) and Conditions Governing Business 7.5(3) (insurers), all outsourcing arrangements must be set out in a written agreement.

question: When the PRA sets and collects periodic fees each year to recover its Annual Funding Requirement, how should the Annual Funding Requirement be defined in terms of the types of regulatory costs it reflects, and what category of budgeted costs must be excluded from that definition?
expected_answer: For the purpose of periodic fees that are set by the PRA and collected each year to recover the PRA’s Annual Funding Requirement, the Annual Funding Requirement should be defined by reference to the cost categories it is intended to recover and the cost categories it expressly does not recover. On the inclusion side, the Annual Funding Requirement reflects the costs relating to Ongoing Regulatory Activities, meaning the costs the PRA incurs in performing its functions as regulator, and it may also reflect exceptional costs (for example, costs arising from recent changes in the scope of regulation) where those exceptional costs are not incorporated into Ongoing Regulatory Activities costs [#SRC:85621563f8cf9168]. On the exclusion side, the Annual Funding Requirement does not include any special project fee costs where those costs are budgeted, so those budgeted special project fee costs must be kept outside the Annual Funding Requirement even though periodic fees are collected to recover it [#TGT:230a19b54b13bd74]. Taken together, this means the Annual Funding Requirement is a funding measure tied to ongoing regulatory and certain exceptional regulatory costs, but it is not a vehicle for recovering budgeted special project fee costs.
source_text: Periodic fees are set by the PRA and collected each year in order to recover the PRA’s Annual Funding Requirement (AFR). The AFR reflects: 1 • costs relating to Ongoing Regulatory Activities (ORA), being the costs which the PRA incurs in performing its functions as regulator; and • any exceptional costs (eg to reflect recent changes in the scope of regulation) not incorporated into ORA costs.
target_text: 1. Note: the AFR does not include any special project fee (SPF) costs, where these are budgeted.

question: For undertakings referred to in the specified category, and excluding undertakings covered by the separate carve-out, what must the equity risk sub-module include when determining the relevant amount under the referenced valuation and standard formula provisions?
expected_answer: For undertakings referred to in the specified category, the scope condition is that the approach applies to those undertakings except where they fall within the separate exclusion for undertakings covered by the carve-out, and the amount is to be determined in accordance with the referenced valuation and standard formula provisions [#SRC:a19de5e5078439a5]. Within that scoped determination, the equity risk sub-module must be structured to include distinct risk sub-modules covering type 1 equities and type 2 equities, and it must also include dedicated risk sub-modules for qualifying infrastructure equities and for qualifying infrastructure corporate equities [#TGT:8a3ef0d20b9b4dac]. In practice, this means that, for an undertaking that is in-scope (i.e., within the referred category and not within the carve-out), the equity risk component cannot be treated as a single undifferentiated charge; it must be decomposed into the four specified equity categories so that the amount determined under the referenced framework reflects each required sub-module. The exclusion matters because undertakings within the carve-out are not subject to this scoped determination pathway [#SRC:a19de5e5078439a5].
source_text: (4) for undertakings referred to in 11.1A(6) , other than undertakings covered by point (5) of this rule, the amount determined in accordance with Valuation 9 and Solvency Capital Requirement – Standard Formula 3D7 - 3D11 , 3D26 – 3D31 and 3D32 ; and
target_text: The equity risk sub-module must include a risk sub-module for type 1 equities, a risk sub-module for type 2 equities, a risk sub-module for qualifying infrastructure equities and a risk sub-module for qualifying infrastructure corporate equities.

question: If an undertaking wants to set up or change a debt securities programme to issue something the firm plans to count as basic own funds for the group SCR, what does the firm have to check about earlier information it gave to the PRA and about changes in law, and what must the programme say about what each instrument issued under it is?
expected_answer: If an undertaking proposes to establish or amend a debt securities programme to issue an item the firm intends to include within the basic own funds forming the own funds eligible for the group SCR, the firm must ensure the programme meets conditions that protect both regulatory compliance and the intended own-funds treatment [#TGT:d43cd8def623245e]. First, the firm must make sure the programme still complies even if there have been changes in law or regulation, or in how those rules are interpreted or applied, since the last time the programme was notified; and the firm must also ensure that the information previously notified to the PRA about the programme is not affected by those changes [#SRC:a0002fe3a6bea784]. Second, the firm must ensure the programme’s terms require that any instrument issued under the programme constitutes basic own funds, so that instruments issued pursuant to the programme match the firm’s intention to include them within basic own funds for group SCR eligibility [#SRC:a0002fe3a6bea784]. Together, these points describe what the firm must ensure when it is proposing to set up or change the programme for that purpose [#TGT:d43cd8def623245e].

question: When providing resolution planning information about the group’s preparations, what must the firm do to ensure it is prepared for an orderly resolution with minimal disruption of critical services, and how should it respond if the PRA and the Bank as resolution authority—after discussing with one or both among the home state supervisor and home resolution authority—determine that additional information is required?
expected_answer: The firm must ensure that its resolution planning materials describe and support concrete preparations that enable the firm to be resolved in an orderly manner, if needed, while minimising disruption to critical services [#TGT:ba7a108ec58f63f0]. In practice, this means the firm’s resolution planning information should cover the group’s preparations for resolution and present them in a way that demonstrates readiness for orderly resolution outcomes, rather than treating the submission as a purely descriptive exercise [#SRC:b277461e673dbd9a]. The firm should also be prepared for supervisory follow-up: the PRA and the Bank as resolution authority may engage with external authorities by discussing the firm’s position with one or both among the home state supervisor and home resolution authority, and then assess whether the firm needs to provide further information [#SRC:b277461e673dbd9a]. Accordingly, the firm should maintain its resolution planning information so it can promptly supply any additional information requested, ensuring that any supplemental materials continue to evidence the firm’s preparedness for resolution and its ability to protect continuity of critical services [#TGT:ba7a108ec58f63f0].
source_text: resolution planning, including information regarding the group’s preparations for resolution consistent with Fundamental Rule 8 (the PRA, and the Bank as resolution authority, will discuss with one or both among the home state supervisor and home resolution authority, and then consider if any additional information is required from the firm).
target_text: Fundamental Rule 8: A firm must prepare for resolution so, if the need arises, it can be resolved in an orderly manner with a minimum disruption of critical services.
